label: Moduli Spaces of Stable Maps
notes: Chapter six builds the compactification that makes Gromov-Witten counting possible. We motivate why smooth J-holomorphic curves alone fail to form a closed space, and how Kontsevich's stable maps repair the gap by allowing nodal domains with finite automorphism groups, yielding a compact metrizable moduli space.

label: Why Compactify
notes: A sequence of embedded spheres can degenerate as energy concentrates, bubbling off lower curves. The limit leaves the smooth stratum, so naive moduli are non-compact. Gromov compactness tells us the limit is a nodal configuration, which we must legitimize as an object of the moduli problem.

label: Stable Maps
notes: A stable map is a nodal genus-g curve with marked points together with a J-holomorphic map, subject to a stability condition: every ghost component must carry enough special points to rigidify it. Stability forces the automorphism group to be finite, which is exactly what compactness and Hausdorffness require.

label: The Moduli Space
notes: We assemble all stable maps of class A, genus g, with n marked points into one set and topologize it by Gromov convergence. The resulting space is compact and metrizable. This single object replaces the open manifold of smooth curves and supports evaluation and forgetful structure maps.

label: Evaluation Maps
notes: Each marked point yields an evaluation map sending a stable map to the image of that point in M. Together the n evaluations form a map to the n-fold product. Pulling back cohomology classes through evaluation is how incidence constraints on curves become integrals over moduli.

label: Forgetful Maps
notes: Forgetting a marked point or the map data defines projections between moduli spaces. After forgetting we must stabilize the domain, contracting any component that has become unstable. These forgetful morphisms organize the spaces into a tower and underlie recursive structures like the string and dilaton equations.

label: Stratification by Domain Type
notes: The moduli space decomposes into strata indexed by the combinatorial type of the domain: the dual graph recording components, nodes, genera, and marked points. The top open stratum has a smooth irreducible domain; deeper strata correspond to more degenerate trees of bubbles glued at nodes.

label: The Boundary
notes: Boundary strata are where domains acquire nodes. The codimension of a stratum grows with the number of nodes, since each node imposes a diagonal matching condition in the target. For meaningful counts these boundary strata must sit in real codimension at least two.

label: Virtual Dimension
notes: The expected dimension comes from the index of the linearized Cauchy-Riemann operator plus the dimension of domain deformations. For genus zero it reads two times the quantity n plus the first Chern number plus the complex dimension minus three. This number is what transverse moduli should realize.

label: Obstructions to Smoothness
notes: Multiple covers and non-transversality prevent the moduli space from being a smooth manifold of the expected dimension. A multiply covered curve can have a cokernel that inflates dimension, so the actual stratum exceeds the virtual count. These obstructions motivate the virtual fundamental class.

label: Virtual Fundamental Class
notes: When transversality fails one builds a virtual fundamental class of the expected dimension, against which Gromov-Witten invariants are defined. The obstruction bundle and an abstract perturbation cut the moduli space down to virtual dimension, restoring well-defined intersection numbers despite singular strata.

label: Genus Zero Semipositive Case
notes: When the manifold is semipositive and the genus is zero, bad bubble strata already have codimension at least two. Transversality for simple maps then makes the evaluation map a pseudocycle, so invariants are honest intersection numbers and the heavy virtual machinery becomes unnecessary.
